questions.questionText: Which process requires energy from ATP?
questions.explanation: Active transport moves molecules against their concentration gradient and requires ATP energy and carrier proteins.

questions.questionText: Osmosis is the movement of:

options.text: Solutes from high to low concentration
Water from high to low water potential

questions.explanation: Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from an area of higher water potential to lower water potential.

questions.questionText: In a hypertonic solution, a plant cell will:
questions.explanation: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves the plant cell by osmosis, causing the protoplast to shrink away from the cell wall (plasmolysis).

questions.questionText: Simple diffusion does not require:
questions.explanation: Simple diffusion is a passive process that moves molecules down the concentration gradient without requiring energy.

questions.questionText: Which type of transport uses carrier proteins?
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins to help large or polar molecules cross the membrane without ATP.

questions.questionText: An isotonic solution has:

options.text: Higher solute concentration than the cell
Lower solute concentration than the cell
Equal solute concentration to the cell

questions.explanation: In isotonic solutions, water moves equally in both directions, so there is no net change in cell volume.

questions.questionText: Endocytosis is used to:

options.text: Bring large particles into the cell

questions.explanation: Endocytosis brings materials into the cell by forming a vesicle from the plasma membrane, including phagocytosis and pinocytosis.

questions.questionText: In an animal cell placed in a hypotonic solution, the cell will:
questions.hint: No cell wall in animal cells.
questions.explanation: Without a cell wall, animal cells in hypotonic solutions swell and burst (osmotic lysis) as water rushes in.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is an example of active transport?
questions.hint: Pump using ATP to move ions.
questions.explanation: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to actively transport 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in against their gradients.

questions.questionText: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion because it:

options.text: Uses carrier or channel proteins for large/polar molecules

questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion uses specific transport proteins to help large, polar molecules cross the membrane without energy input.

questions.questionText: The sodium-potassium pump exchanges:
questions.explanation: For every ATP used, the sodium-potassium pump transports 3 sodium ions out and 2 potassium ions in, establishing the resting membrane potential.

questions.questionText: Phagocytosis specifically refers to:
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis (cell eating) engulfs large solid particles like bacteria into phagosomes for digestion.

questions.questionText: Aquaporins are:
questions.explanation: Aquaporins are specialised channel proteins that facilitate the rapid diffusion of water across membranes.

questions.questionText: Pinocytosis is important for:

options.text: Uptake of extracellular fluids and dissolved nutrients

questions.explanation: Pinocytosis (cell drinking) engulfs extracellular fluids and dissolved solutes into vesicles for cellular intake.

questions.questionText: Turgor pressure in plant cells is maintained by:

options.text: Water moving into the vacuole by osmosis
Active transport of minerals out of the cell

questions.explanation: Water enters the central vacuole by osmosis, creating turgor pressure that pushes the protoplast against the rigid cell wall.

questions.questionText: In the sodium-potassium pump, phosphorylation of the pump protein:

options.text: Is caused by binding of sodium ions
Causes a conformational change that releases Na+
Is the first step in the cycle

questions.explanation: ATP hydrolysis adds a phosphate group to the pump protein, causing it to change shape and release Na+ before binding K+.

questions.questionText: Receptor-mediated endocytosis is highly specific because:

options.text: Only one type of molecule can fit into any vesicle
Specific receptor proteins on the membrane bind only target ligands
Vesicles are always the same size

questions.explanation: Specific transmembrane receptors bind only their target ligands (e.g., LDL, transferrin), ensuring selective and efficient uptake.

questions.questionText: Why do plant cells not burst in hypotonic solutions while animal cells do?

options.text: Plant cells have a rigid cell wall that resists expansion

questions.explanation: The rigid cell wall prevents the plant cell from expanding beyond its limit, so instead of bursting, it becomes turgid.

questions.questionText: The rate of diffusion is affected by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Diffusion rate depends on temperature, concentration gradient, surface area, distance, and molecular size. Colour does not affect diffusion rate.

questions.questionText: Exocytosis and endocytosis are both:

options.text: Forms of bulk transport requiring energy

questions.explanation: Both endocytosis and exocytosis require ATP energy to form and move vesicles, making them forms of active bulk transport.
